feel borrowed.article:
# One Office, Two Ideas of a Place to Work

## The Question

Every morning, one employee enters the office and looks for an empty desk. Another chooses a quiet corner or a lively place near other teams. Some companies are bringing back assigned desks, while others continue shared seating. Why can the same office feel secure to one person and liberating to another?

### One Voice: The desk that lets work begin

Every morning, I look for an empty desk. Someone else may have used it yesterday, and someone new may sit there tomorrow. I cannot leave papers in a drawer, and I sometimes worry about using a desk or keyboard after someone else. Before work begins, I have already spent time finding a place. I miss the same desk, drawer, and view. They helped me start without searching and gave me a quiet sense of belonging. Now the office can feel borrowed. I want my work and things to have a place, even when I cannot choose the seating policy.

### Another Voice: The freedom to move

Some mornings, I choose a quiet corner because I need to think. On other days, I sit where conversation is easy. A different desk can bring me closer to people from another department. It can also give me distance when a workplace relationship feels uncomfortable or when I simply need room. Since working from home gave me a place of my own, I do not need one fixed spot at the office. I value being able to change my surroundings and choose a place that fits my mood, my task, and the people I need—or do not need—around me.

## Where the Difference Comes From

The disagreement is not really about movement. It is about where stability comes from. One employee finds it in a desk that stays put, with papers and a familiar start. The other finds it in the power to change social distance and the kind of space needed that day. A shared-seat system can even create unofficial regular desks. So a rule that looks flexible on paper may feel like friction to one person, while the same system feels useful to another.

## What the Seat Really Means

The real question is not fixed desks or shared desks. It is what makes a place workable: a stable point that removes daily searching, or enough control to change one’s social and working surroundings. The seat is only the visible part of a deeper question: what makes an employee feel, “This is my place at work”?

# “Cockroach Milk”: Before You Get a Cup, Look at How It Stores Food

If you hear “cockroach milk,” the café in your mind shuts down. I understand. But let’s put the urgent meeting about drinking it on hold. The story is not its taste or how it feels to swallow. It is how baby cockroaches store food just for themselves.

The Ig Nobel Prize went to earlier research on crystals full of nutrients. This does not mean cockroach milk has finally appeared on the dinner table! No one drank it as part of the study. The study did not test it as food for people. Put the cup back on the shelf.

The study looked at a kind of cockroach that keeps its babies inside its body. Researchers took protein crystals with nutrients from the gut of the unborn young. You may think you are heading to the milk aisle. Instead, you see the food store inside a body.

The researchers used X-rays to study the shape of the protein inside the crystals. Fats stuck to the protein, and sugars stuck to it too. You may have expected a fancy latte. Instead, you got a map of molecules. Suddenly, we are in a science lab.

The paper gives a surprising estimate. The crystals have over three times as much energy as the same weight of milk. The milk came from several kinds of mammals.

“The final boss of nutrition?”

The marketing team may be ready to jump into action, but wait. The comparison was between “crystals” and “milk.” It does not mean that drinking them would make people three times as energetic. Take that number alone, and soon a science story can turn into a TV shopping show.

The more interesting idea is turning nutrients into crystals and storing them away. No fridge, no lunch box. If tiny crystals can store food, that is a clever way to save space.

The authors also say storing nutrients as crystals may help feed the young. But this role has not been confirmed. Next to “That makes sense!” there should be a sign saying “Still being studied.” The two should be shown together.

When you hear “packed with nutrition,” ask, “Compared with what?” and “For whom?” Behind the exciting number, you may find something else that is interesting.

Do not see this as a possible breakfast for people. See it as a way to bring nutrients to the young. They have not been born yet. You do not need to be brave enough to drink it. Today, bring your curiosity, not a cup. Look inside this little food store.

## In one line
Researchers studied protein crystals with nutrients in unborn cockroach babies, not cockroach milk for people. The crystals may help feed the babies, but this is not confirmed.

story with two different speeds.article:
# Young Japanese Travelers Want More Freedom, But Their Trips Are Still Short

As of September 2026, travel surveys in Japan tell a story with two different speeds.

Many younger travelers, especially men, seem to want more room for their own pace and interests. But the trips measured in surveys are still short.

This contrast appears clearly when people imagine having more time. In one survey, the most common answer was about one week of travel if people could take a one-month vacation. About 24% chose that answer.

But an autumn survey by the same research center asked about people considering a trip. Their planned stays averaged about 1.8 nights, with a median of about two nights.

These were not the same question. One measured a wish under a special condition. The other measured a current travel plan. Together, they show a gap between the trip people imagine and the time they plan to spend.

Japan’s Tourism White Paper also says the country needs more trips per person and longer stays. In other words, longer travel is still a policy goal, not a completed change in behavior.

So this is not a simple story about famous sightseeing being replaced by slow travel. The clearer story is that attitudes are changing faster than travel schedules.

### Slow travel is also about control

Slow travel here may mean control over time, not simply more nights. Men aged 29 and under put solo travel at 25.2%, while hobby-focused travel showed a similar pattern. Separately, about 90% of Gen Z respondents wanted free time during an overseas tour, and about 80% wanted half a day or more. A short package does not have to be fully scheduled.

### One youth market does not fit all

“Young Japanese travelers” is too broad a label. For men aged 18 to 29, solo travel was the leading travel arrangement in another survey. But among women aged 29 and under, 44.7% were still interested in visiting famous tourist spots. Different groups may respond to different offers: flexible, interest-led plans for some, and landmark-focused trips for others.

## In one line…

Young travelers in Japan are showing a clearer wish for more self-directed travel, especially young men, but the evidence points to an emerging preference—not a completed shift to longer stays.

keep one's eyes on them.sent: The ruler kept his eyes on them
keep one's eyes on them.article:
Melos called across the hall, “You kill men from fear. You never give them a chance to speak.”

Silence came, and guards grabbed the young shepherd. The ruler ordered his death.

“Give me three days to see my sister’s wedding,” Melos said. “Then I will return to you.”

The ruler smiled and said, “Your friend must stay here. Return late, and he will die in your place.”

Melos turned to his friend, who offered his hands for the chains. Melos had no time to speak.

“Go now, because I know you will come back.”

At the wedding, his sister’s laugh rose above everyone’s voices. Melos listened closely to remember its exact sound.

He left for the city before daylight on day three.

The river stopped him; its bridge was gone. Rain made the water brown and dangerously fast. He stepped back, ran, and jumped into the flood.

The water pulled him under, but he fought toward the light. He grabbed a branch and pulled himself onto the far bank.

Later, three men blocked his way, and a knife flashed. He hit the man holding it with his walking stick. He ran uphill as their shouts followed behind him.

By afternoon, each step hurt, and his feet were bloody. He fell beside a rock and tried to stand. But his legs would not lift him.

He could wait here, and someone might find him. Or he could return home.

But his friend would lose his life instead.

For one awful moment, that felt easier than standing up.

He remembered the hands held out for the chains. His friend trusted him without asking for another promise.

Water came slowly through a crack in the rock. Melos drank, got onto his knees, and stood up.

He managed one step, then took another.

At the city gates, the bell rang for his friend’s death.

He raced to the square, where the sword was already raised above his friend.

“Stop now! I’m back!”

His friend turned around, and Melos fell against him.

“I almost left you to die,” he said softly.

“I almost lost my trust in you,” his friend replied.

They held each other while the last sun lit the walls.

The ruler kept his eyes on them.

Finally, he said, “Put the sword down and free both men.”

More softly, he then asked, “How can a man win such trust?”

For once, he waited for a reply instead of demanding one.

legs fail someone.article:
The guards stopped moving as Melos began to speak.

“You give people no fair trial before killing them,” he told the ruler. “If someone scares you, you order his death.”

The shepherd faced the ruler alone in dusty sandals, trying to hide his fear.

The ruler narrowed his eyes. “You will die too.”

His stomach felt tight.

“May I have three days for my sister’s wedding?” he asked. “Then I'll come back.”

Laughing, the ruler asked, “Back to die?”

“My friend can take my place here.”

His friend silently stepped up. The ruler watched both as if looking for a trick.

“Return before sunset on day three,” he finally said. “Your friend dies if you're late.”

His friend’s warm, steady fingers closed around Melos’s hand.

“Leave now. I'll wait for you.”

His sister’s smiles made Melos smile at her wedding. He watched her take her husband’s hands. But he looked at the door whenever a shadow crossed the floor. Time moved on.

He left for the city before dawn on day three.

He stopped walking at the river.

There was no bridge left.

Brown water rushed through the crossing with broken branches. Rain had flooded the river. He searched the banks but found no other crossing.

Melos took a step into the river.

The current knocked him down, filling his mouth with muddy water. He fought towards the far bank, reaching for a passing branch. He caught it, held tight, and pulled himself ashore.

Shaking, he got up and ran on.

Past the river, attackers blocked his way. One grabbed his arm; another swung a stick. Melos hit back, escaped, and stumbled past. They shouted angrily behind him, but he never looked back.

Every step hurt by that afternoon.

His legs suddenly failed him.

On the ground, face down, he could not even stand. The distant city was still beyond reach.

Perhaps he could stay here.

Until sunset, nobody would find him. He would live, although his friend would die.

For one terrible moment, that idea made him feel better.

Then he remembered his friend’s warm fingers holding his hand.

“I'll wait for you.”

Now his friend listened for footsteps as he waited.

Melos raised his head.

A little water ran between nearby stones. He drank, rose to his knees, then stood with shaking legs.

Once more, he started to run.

With the sun sinking, he reached the city, pushing through the crowd.

His friend stood, wrists tied. The executioner lifted his sword.

“Wait, please!”

He fell down at his friend’s feet.

“I've come back!”

The sword moved no further.

Laughing and crying, his friend bent over Melos. Reaching up, Melos held him tightly.

“I almost stopped trying,” he whispered.

“You came back, though.”

Watching their joined hands, the ruler finally ordered the guards to free both men.

“I thought everyone would save himself,” he said.

Their hands stayed together.

For the first time, the ruler’s words were not an order.

“Can you show me how to trust?”

one's face harden.article:
In a small kingdom, the ruler, Dionysius, was afraid of enemies. If anyone spoke against him, his guards could take that person to prison. Often, the ruler ordered executions without a fair trial.

One day, a shepherd named Melos stood before him.

“You punish people before you know the truth,” Melos said. “That is not justice.”

The ruler’s face became hard. “Then you will die.”

Melos’s sister was going to be married in three days. He fell to his knees.

“Please let me go to her wedding,” he said. “I will return before my death.”

The ruler laughed. “Why should I believe you?”

Melos’s friend, Selinuntius, stepped forward. “I will stay here in his place.”

So the ruler agreed. Melos had three days to go and return. If he did not come back, his friend would die.

Melos ran from the city. He reached the river, but heavy rain had made the water wild. The small boat broke against a rock. Melos fell into the cold river and nearly disappeared under the water. At last, he reached the other side, shaking and weak.

He hurried to the wedding. He smiled for his sister, but his eyes stayed on the road. When the wedding ended, he left at once.

On the way back, three attackers jumped from behind some trees. They took his horse and pushed him to the ground. Melos tried to stand, but pain filled his body. He walked through the night, then fell beside the road.

The sky was becoming bright. The time was almost finished.

Melos looked toward the city. “I cannot do this,” he whispered. “Perhaps my friend is already dead.”

For a moment, he wanted to hide in the forest.

Then he remembered his friend’s calm face. His friend had trusted him enough to face death.

“No,” Melos said. “I gave my word.”

He stood and ran.

At the city gate, the guards were leading his friend to the place of execution. Then Melos shouted, “Wait!”

Everyone turned. Melos fell before the ruler.

“I promised to return,” he said. “I am here.”

The ruler looked at the two friends. Slowly, he lowered his hand.

“Free him,” he said.

After that day, the ruler demanded fair trials. He had learned that trust and loyalty could be stronger than fear.

sheltered from the rain.sent: Bob stood in the doorway of a closed hardware store, sheltered from the rain
sheltered from the rain.article:
Bob stood in the doorway of a closed hardware store, sheltered from the rain. It was almost ten. He shifted his unlit cigar between his teeth and looked down the street. Twenty years was a long time, but he had not forgotten the place.

A patrolman stopped beside him.

“Just waiting for a friend,” Bob explained. “There used to be a restaurant here.”

“They pulled it down five years ago.”

Bob struck a match. The flame lit his face as he raised it to his cigar.

“We had our last dinner there twenty years ago tonight. My best friend, Jimmy. We grew up together, like brothers.”

The patrolman listened calmly while rain tapped against the pavement.

“I went West,” Bob continued. “Jimmy stayed here. He thought New York was the only place worth living. Before we parted, we promised to meet here at ten tonight, whatever happened.”

“Have you heard from him?”

“Not for years. We lost touch.” Bob smiled. “Still, a promise meant something to Jimmy. He’ll come if he’s alive.”

“How long will you wait?”

“Half an hour.”

“Well, I hope he turns up. Good night.”

The patrolman walked on.

Bob leaned against the doorway, listening for footsteps. Once, he took out his watch, then slipped it away again. He had travelled too far to worry about a few minutes.

At half past ten, a tall man in a long overcoat hurried towards him.

“Is that you, Bob?”

“Jimmy!”

The man caught both his hands. Bob laughed with relief. For a moment, they seemed young again, with their whole lives ahead of them.

They set off arm in arm. Bob talked eagerly about the West, his business and the money he had made. After twenty years, there was almost too much to say.

Then they passed a drugstore. Light from its windows fell across their faces.

Bob stopped and pulled his arm free.

“You’re not Jimmy. Twenty years can change a man, but not the shape of his nose.”

“They can change a good man into a bad one,” the tall man replied. “You’re under arrest, Bob. You’re wanted in Chicago.”

Bob stared at him.

“Before we go, there’s a note for you.”

Bob unfolded it under the bright window.

“Bob, it’s Jimmy. I was the patrolman you spoke to. I came on time to keep our promise. When you struck that match, I recognized your face as the man wanted in Chicago. But I couldn’t bring myself to arrest my old friend, so I found a plain-clothes officer to do it for me.”

smile through one's tears.sent: She pressed them to her chest and smiled through her tears
smile through one's tears.article:
Della counted her coins again, pressing them against the table. She still had only $1.87, and Christmas was tomorrow.

She had saved every coin she could for Jim, her husband. How could she buy him a good enough gift?

She cried for a while on their old couch. Then she noticed her face in the mirror.

They were proud of two things: Della’s long brown hair and Jim’s gold watch. His grandfather, then his father, had owned the watch before him.

She slowly let down her hair, shining below her knees. She ran her fingers through it in the pale light. Quickly, she put on her coat before changing her mind.

Outside a shop selling hair, she stopped to catch her breath.

“Would you like to buy my hair?”

The shop owner lifted her thick waves of hair.

“I can pay you twenty dollars.”

“Please cut it off right now.”

Della closed her eyes as the scissors first touched her hair.

For two hours, she rushed between shops until she found it: a simple platinum watch chain. Like Jim, it needed nothing extra to show its value.

Its price was twenty-one dollars.

With eighty-seven cents left, she took it home. She pictured Jim using it instead of his worn leather strap.

By seven, dinner was almost ready, and her short hair was curled. Still, she kept looking in the mirror.

“Please, let me still look pretty to him,” she said softly.

She heard his steps, and then the door opened.

Jim stood still in the doorway.

He stared at her hair as she hurried towards him.

“Jim, I sold my hair to buy you a Christmas gift. It will grow back!”

He held her close, then handed her a package.

She found the tortoise-shell combs inside the package. She had often admired them in a shop window.

She pressed them to her chest and smiled through her tears.

“It won’t take long for my hair to grow.”

Then she remembered her gift and took out the chain.

“See how beautiful it is! Let me have your watch.”

Jim smiled softly as he took a seat.

“To buy your combs, I had to sell my watch.”

Della joined him and held his hand. Without her hair, she could not use the combs. Without his watch, he could not use the chain. Both had sold their greatest treasure for the other’s gift.

Wise men called the magi brought gifts on the first Christmas. The two young people seemed foolish with their useless gifts. But their love made them wiser than all other gift-givers. In every place, they are the wisest; these two are the magi.
